newsitem.title: USA: U.S. September wholesale inventories drop sharply.
newsitem.headline: U.S. September wholesale inventories drop sharply.

text.p: Inventories of goods on wholesalers' shelves dropped at the sharpest rate in 14-1/2 years during September, the Commerce Department said on Friday, as sales picked up from an August slump.
Overall inventories fell 1.3 percent to a seasonally adjusted $255.52 billion -- the biggest monthly decline since a 1.6 percent plunge in February 1982, the department said.
The sharp inventory drop was contrary to Wall Street economists' forecast for a 0.3 percent September increase in inventories.
In addition, August inventories were revised to show a 0.1 percent decrease -- instead of the 0.5 percent rise in unsold stocks that the governemnt had reported a month ago.
Total wholesale sales increased 0.9 percent in September to $201.97 billion after falling a revised 1 percent in August. Previously, the department said August sales had declined 0.9 percent.
As a result, the inventory-to-sales ratio, which measures how long it would take to deplete inventories at the current sales pace, fell to 1.27 months' worth from 1.29 months in August.
That was the lowest level for the inventory-to-sales ratio in more than six years, since it was also at 1.27 months' worth in August 1990.
Stocks of both durable and nondurable goods were drawn down in September.
There was a big 4 percent drop in motor vehicle and equipment inventories from August levels and smaller declines in electrical goods and metals.
Similarly, inventories of nondurables like farm-product raw materials, groceries and clothing fell sharply.

The Commerce Department previously reported that third-quarter economic growth slowed sharply to a 2.2 percent annual rate from 4.7 percent in the second quarter. Weaker stock-building is consistent with a moderating economy.
Lower rates of inventory-building put a drag on growth because it means that not as many goods are being produced.
